utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam. Today is Wednesday, October 22nd, 2008. Good morning to Ms. Biersay, Mr. Mundis, their case manager, as well as Mr. Seselj and everyone in this courtroom. We are going to have the witness brought in, Ms. Tabeau.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Ms. Tabeau. We are going to proceed with the cross-examination, and I'm going to give the floor to Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau, I'm going to start with a question, but it's a bit more extensive, and I'm not going to resort to that again. After that, my questions will be very short, so please listen to me very carefully. I will try to present a paradigm here, showing a proper methodological approach that would be applied by a serious scholar who were to be given the assignment you got, the emigration of Croats and other non-Serbs from Hrtkovci in 1992. If you listen to me carefully, I'm going to ask you if you agree with this paradigm of a methodological approach. If a serious scientist or scholar were to be given this assignment, he would first -- he or she would first have to acquaint himself or herself with socio-political circumstances that have to be resolved. This person would see that a state existed there that was called Yugoslavia and that it broke apart in a bloody civil war, also that some Croats moved out of Serbia to Croatia. Serbia and Croatia were federal units of that former country of Yugoslavia. So, in order for the methodological approach to be the right one, a serious scientist would take into account the following data: A statistical review of the census, the latest census in Croatia, that is to say, from 1991; a statistical review of the national population of Serbia in 1991; and then that person would see how many declared Croats lived in Serbia and how many declared Serbs lived in Croatia. Then he or she would take the Croatian census from 2001, I believe it was, and the 2002 census in Serbia; and then this person would look at the number of Croats living in Serbia in 2002 and the number of Serbs living in Croatia. And on the basis of that, the said person could draw a preliminary conclusion. Would you agree with this methodological approach as being a right one?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as a starting point, yes, of course; but as we discussed yesterday, this approach would be biased by the changing perceptions of ethnicity between 1991 and 2002 or 2001, the census in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How did this perception of ethnicity change? Could you explain that?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we discussed yesterday, some people declared themselves in different ways between 1991 and 2002, and this has, of course, impact on statistics presented on the basis of the census data.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Ms. Tabeau. You've just said something that had escaped me. There was a census in 1991. Apparently, according to Mr. Seselj - and he's probably checked that - apparently, there was a census in Croatia in 2001 and a census in 2002 in Serbia. But you've just said something that I find rather disturbing. You say that there may have been a change or a changing perception in the way people declared their ethnicity. Let's take the example of someone who declared himself as a Croat; whereas, he could have declared himself as a Serb. Others, apparently, declared themselves as Serbs; whereas, they could have declared themselves as Croats. Is it what you have just said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I rather had in mind the Yugoslavs and the changes in perceptions of Yugoslavs at the time in both countries, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, for the Yugoslavs, it's quite understandable. But could the same thing have happened for Croats or Serbs who may have decided to declare themselves Croats because their names sound Croat, or someone may have decided to declare himself as a Serb because he has a Serb cousin? In other words, have you identified cases of people who declared themselves as belonging to a certain ethnicity; whereas, it was not that clear-cut?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is possible for any ethnic group, most certainly for Croats and Serbs, but I would expect that for Yugoslavs, the numbers of these changing perceptions would be higher than for other ethnic groups. So I would expect that we wouldn't see many cases of Croats reporting themselves as Serbs in Vojvodina; and, on the other hand, in Croatia, the same thing for Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to be more specific in my question. We've heard evidence suggesting that there were mixed marriages, and no one can deny that there were mixed marriages. Let's take the case of a Serb -- of a wedding between a Serb and a Croat. Let's take the case of the child of this couple, who has a Serb mother and a Croatian father. A census happens, this child is asked what ethnic group he belongs to. What is going to be the answer, Croat, Serb, Yugoslav, maybe 1991? How can you approach that type of situation in statistics? Does that produce a margin of error in the statistic, because I'm sure that that type of cases may have happened. Some people may have decided to report themselves as Croats or Serbs; whereas, they could have decided to do exactly the opposite.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, most certainly, it has impact on statistics. In the case of this particular family, with parents being one Croat, another Serb, any option is possible. The child could have been reported as a Croat, as a Serb, a Serbo-Croat, or a Yugoslav. Anything is possible. In order to quantify the impact of the reporting and the changing perceptions, it is necessary to work with individual data and to link individuals reported in 1991 census with the record of the same person in the 2002 census. And by comparing reporting on the individual level, it is possible to quantify the impact of changes in perceptions of ethnicity. I couldn't do it, and I don't think it is possible by using aggregate census statistics as published. So this approach Mr. Seselj mentioned is biased, whether he wants it or not. It is not a good starting point, anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, talking about this individual perception and individual choices, in cases such as the ones identified by the Presiding Judge, you are talking about an individual choice. But this choice, wasn't it influenced by your faith, by the fact that the person was Orthodox or Catholic? That's the result of the choice of your parents when you are born, when they decide what sort of religion you're going to belong to. So would that choice be -- depend on your religion? In other words, ethnicity is very much connected to religion .

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before you answer, let me add this to the question put to you by my colleague: Witnesses here told us that in the previous system, in the communist system, Catholics didn't want anyone to know that they were Catholics because it was -- it could be detrimental for them. Therefore, this religious factor mentioned by my fellow Judge, could it have an impact during the census of 1991, when the country was still in existence? Did you take that into account as a demographer, that people, for religious reasons, the ones identified by my fellow Judges, that people may have decided to choose a specific ethnic group, but that because of the political system in place, they were not in a position to declare themselves freely because it was not such a good idea under the existing system? Well, did you take all this into account?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is a high correspondence between ethnicity and religion, but there is no one-to-one correspondence. I studied this using the census data for Bosnia and Herzegovina, and it is not that every Croat is Catholic and every Serb is Orthodox, but the correlation of these two is extremely high. So one of the main components of identifying a person as being a Croat, Serb, Hungarian, is religion; and, of course, Croats would be mainly Catholics and Serbs mainly Orthodox. But ethnicity is a broader term. It is not only religion that is one of the component dimensions of ethnicity. It is generally the cultural, common history, common language, common traditions, and so on and so on. Of course, there were studies of ethnicity using all kinds of definitions. There were studies that have taken religion as the major and only component of ethnicity, but it is broader than that. How people report themselves in the census, well, this is a good question. I believe that religion is the main determining factor, but there are also other factors; and especially in politically unstable times, economically unstable times, people take into account the situation. They do what is better for them. I wouldn't think that this had a major impact on my study on Hrtkovci. I think, in this case, the Catholic population of Hrtkovci was mainly Croats and Hungarians. This is how it was. So I think in this particular case, the religion is a good proxy for ethnicity, simply speaking, yeah. I hope I answered the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Madam Tabeau, did you come across any information that would suggest that people could register themselves as Yugoslav as a result of a deliberate political determination not to be associated with any of the ethnical groups in the former Yugoslavia; that is to say, somebody, even though he perhaps was born by Serb parents and was Orthodox by religion, he would, for political reasons, not wish to declare him or herself as a Serb? Could that also be part of the group of Yugoslavs registered in your review?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't study this for Vojvodina and Hrtkovci because this would require that I had at least the individual data from the two censuses, 1991 and 2002; and then, empirically, I could compare and check these kind of situations. I did study the data for Bosnia. Well, I didn't have the second census for Bosnia because we haven't had the census in Bosnia yet, after the census in 1991. But there is -- there are a lot of sources on war victims that report ethnicity as well, and then you see clearly cases of changing ethnicity in relation to the ethnicity reported in the 1991 census. Then Yugoslavs would be reported as victims of a concrete ethnic group; well, but this is a totally situation. You are speaking here of a surviving population, people who are alive and want to have a good life. So this is not really comparable to the example I mentioned. Well, so it's better not to speculate in this case, right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you may proceed. I hope that we have not encroached on any issues you, yourself, wanted to raise during your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You brought up many questions now, but I'll make an effort to remember all of them and, in a way, to have the witness clarify each and every one of these questions, to the extent possible, of course. This is very complex subject matter, and I hope that you will grant my request to give me more time for cross-examination. I will only deal with the expert report from a professional point of view. I won't go into anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau, you mentioned something here that had to do with the change in the way citizens were declaring themselves ethnically. You mentioned that as an argument against my paradigm of a methodological approach, the one that I referred to. You said that that methodological approach would be applicable if it weren't for that. However, there's another thing that has to be taken into account. According to the 1991 census, there is between 600.000 and 700.000 declared Serbs in Croatia and about 300.000 declared Yugoslavs; and then there's the latest census in Croatia, stating that there is somewhat less than 200.000 Serbs in Croatia. This must have impressed you, this difference, this decline in the number of Serbs, because on the one hand you have only 15.000 or 16.000 Croats, right? On the one hand, you have half a million Serbs and the Yugoslavs disappeared. We don't know where they disappeared, although there's literature devoted to that subject, too. Then, on the other hand, the difference or number of Croats is only 15.000 or 16.000 between 1991 and 2002. Am I not right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The number of Serbs in the 1991 census is 570.000 or, say, about 580.000. It is not 600 or 700. I have here in front of me the published statistics from the 1991 census, and I can give you the specific numbers. So let's stick to the published statistics. It is 580.000, approximately, Serbs in 1991. And in the year 2001, there was indeed about 200.000 Serbs in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That's roughly 600.000, isn't it? It's roughly 600.000, and now you have 200.000, so not half a million, but the difference is 400.000. So what is it that you think I've not said properly? I have. I have a recollection of the facts. But the figure of 400.000 Serbs who had disappeared must have made an impression on you. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is 380, the difference between the two censuses. It is a lot, of course, of individuals, and it is not about impressing me with any number of this kind because it is a tragic number, simply speaking, if you think of the consequences of this change. Okay. You mentioned also some other numbers, just speaking about the literature, and the difference of Croats, you were saying, is 15.000, 16.000. I wouldn't know what literature, so I can't comment on this. I can give you the change in the number of the Croats according to the census, but I believe it is not what you wanted to say. So please clarify on the Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Tabeau, we all seem to agree now that in Croatia, the number of Serbs diminished between the two censuses of 1991 and 2002, so it declined by 380.000. 380.000 Serbs left Croatia to go somewhere else. This is a fact that has been established, and no one can challenge it because this is something you can see in the census. But there's something I would like to know because I need to know this in order to understand this. Between the two censuses in 1991 and 2002 in Vojvodina, how many Croats left Vojvodina to go to Croatia or somewhere else? How many Croats are we talking about? We need to have that figure in order to compare statistics.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we can do this based on the census data exactly the same way we have done just now for Croatia, knowing that these numbers are not perfect and biased by certain factors. I made a table which is included in my report, and all this data is there in the report. So if you have my report in front of you, please take a look at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please give us the page number?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is page 12 in the English version, table 2. This table contains statistics, aggregate statistics, from two censuses, the 1991 census and the 2002 census.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that really has no sense. The other table -- oh, that's a picture. Right, right. My mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you were mistaken. Yes, please proceed, Madam Tabeau.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the paragraph after -- on the next page, after the four charts, group of charts, four charts, there is a paragraph just at the bottom of these charts in which I discuss the change in the ethnic composition. In this paragraph, I am saying there is 16.000 of Croats that are less in the 2002 census, compared with 1991. I want to mention, we are speaking of a population of Vojvodina, which is much smaller than the population of Croatia, and this is only two million people, approximately. When it comes to the Croatian population in Vojvodina, it is about 72 and a half -- 73.000 individuals in the 1991 census, as compared to approximately 57.000 in 2002 census. This is the Croats only, so it is a small group of people, basically speaking, that was reported in 1991, and this group became even smaller in 2002. I would also like to draw your attention to Hungarians. This is a bigger population. It was a bigger population and is a bigger population in Vojvodina. This population in 1991 was more than 300.000, 333.000 of people, and became 290.000. So here the decline is, in absolute terms, larger. It is a decline of about 43.000 people. These are also non-Serbs. I'm not speaking about the Yugoslavs. Their decline is the highest in this group, but I don't think it is necessary to include them at this stage among the non-Serbs. But as to these two groups, Croats and Hungarians, which are also the groups that I analysed in my report, these are the Catholics in the village, and here are Catholics in the province.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the transcript and for the sake of clarity, let me say the following: The 380.000 Serbs left Croatia to go to Serbia and somewhere else. But based on the table we see at page 12 of your report, we find that 16.000 Croats left Vojvodina, 15.982 exactly. I did my math. So about 16.000 Croats left Vojvodina, and that's something I'd not quite grasped. Hungarians registered a decline of 43.000 people. So we have three times as much Hungarians who left Vojvodina than Croats, 43.000 Hungarians, because at the beginning there were 333.290, and in 2002 you only have 290.000 of them. So when you do your math, you see that there is a difference of 43.000 Hungarians. That's the figures and the statistics we can derive from the census data. A demographer, whether belonging to the OTP or whether being a Serb demographer, would end up with the exact same figures. These figures can't be challenged, Madam Tabeau. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, with one more remark. The timing of departures of both groups is not the same. In Croatia, there were two waves of departures of Croatian Serbs, in 1991, basically, and 1992, and later after Operation Storm and Flash, which would be 1995 and the beginning of 1996. The major wave of these 380.000 is after 1995, summer 1995; whereas, when it comes to Croats from Vojvodina, they were leaving mainly in 1992 and perhaps end of 1991, beginning of 1993. But that is the timing. So the timing is an important factor in the analysis of this figure. If this expert wouldn't take this into account, so then the starting point based on the official data would be wrong, simply, without mentioning the timing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just have one question, and then I will give the floor to my fellow Judge. I've just discovered that we have also a Hungarian question, with 43.000 Hungarians who left between 1991 and 2002. In the indictment, Hungarians are also mentioned. There's not only mention of Croats, but also Hungarians. So why is it that you didn't go into detail when it came to Hungarians? You focused your study on the Croats and didn't really look into the problem of the Hungarians, even though they're three times more numerous. Is there a reason for that, or is it because the Prosecutor didn't really ask you to focus on this population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I did focus on Hungarians as well. In the title of my report, you can read it, it's "The Out-Migration of Croats and other Non-Serbs," and the other non-Serbs are Hungarians in the first place. And in all analysis I made in this report, it is all ethnic groups. I looked at all the ethnic groups and the Hungarians in the first place as non-Serbs, and the parish records I used represent mainly Croats and Hungarians. So I think my report should be read not only as a discussion of statistics on Croats, but on both Croats and Hungarians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you've just raised another question on these church records, these parish records. So regarding the Catholics, there was no difference made between Croats or Hungarians. They were Catholics in the first place; right? The priests in the parish in Vojvodina and some village, when he saw Catholic parents come who wanted to baptize their child, I assume that -- I wonder whether he was asking them, "Are you Croats, Serbs, or Hungarians," or something, or was he just asking, "Are you Catholic," and that's it? So in the parish records, there would only be the names and no reference to the ethnicity of this family, Hungarian or Croat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right. The church books don't specifically report ethnicity. The names are there, and, to a certain extent, ethnicity can be judged, but not, you know -- this is not that name is an expression of ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So all the conclusions drawn from these parish records could involve either Croats or Hungarians, but we don't know whether they are one or the other, unless you try to make a specific analysis from the names. Do we agree with this? All the conclusions drawn from these parish records can mix Croats and Hungarians as Catholics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They are both Croats and Hungarians. I don't distinguish using the parish records, how many are Croats, how many are Hungarians. However, what is indicative of ethnicity is their country of destination, and there is a table in my report in which I show where they went to, these people who departed from Hrtkovci. You will see this from this table. We can refer to this table right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before dealing with the table, I believe my fellow Judge had a question, and we should listen to her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Tabeau, I have the following problem: The absolute figures cannot give us a very specific idea of those who left -- of the comparison of those who left Croatia and those who left Vojvodina. So wouldn't it have been better to give these figures in percentage rather than in absolute figures? Vojvodina has a very limited number of inhabitants, a limited number of non-Serbs; whereas, in Croatia, there were more Serbs in absolute terms, in absolute figures .

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I include also a lot of figures in the report. It is the same table 2, second panel. However, here, in my table, only ethnic composition is shown. But based on the data from the table, relative measures of what fraction of Croats left can be obtained as well. So it's all there in the report. It all can be calculated, so it can be done. But I have one important remark as well. At the level of Vojvodina, the change in the ethnic composition is minor. You can't see what really happened from statistics for the entire province. It is exactly the same situation in Bosnia. If you look at the ethnic composition in the entire country, before the conflict and after the conflict, there is hardly any change at all. Does this mean there were no changes in the ethnic composition in these areas? There were enormous changes, and there were millions of people who left the country or were displaced within the country. So approximately 50 per cent of Bosnia was either displaced or refugees in other countries. So what is really meaningful is to understand what was happening in smaller places, within municipalities, within settlements, within villages and towns such as Hrtkovci. So, in the report, I have two tables: Table 1 for Hrtkovci alone, which is a small village, two and a half thousand people; and Vojvodina as a province, as an entire area. If you look at the province, well, you can think, oh, what is the 16.000 of Croats? It's an important number because the Croats were not uniformly distributed over the province. They were living in concentrations in certain places. Hrtkovci was one of the places. What was happening and what is responsible for the 16.000 is a number, not high number of smaller places, where the changes were really dramatic. This is what I'm showing for Hrtkovci as an example and a representative example of several other places within Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me -- well, look at table 9, page 23 in the English version. Maybe we could have it on the screen. It's the table we saw yesterday and everybody asked questions on it, where we have the departures as of May 8, May 10, May 12, May 13, and a peak on the 15th of May and June 10th. Could we have that on the screen, please? Page 23 in your report. It's table 9.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I think it was also marked as MFI P571.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, P571, MFI. Unfortunately, we don't have the table on the screen yet. It's coming. That's not the one.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: It's on the third page, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 23 in the English report. Yes, now we have it. Madam Tabeau, yesterday, when I put questions to you regarding this table, you told us that this was a table that had been drawn up from the parish records using the christening certificates, if I'm not mistaken. But you just told us a minute ago that there could be Croats and Hungarians here. So I believe that in this table 9, these figures represent both Croats and Hungarians. You agree with me; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. These are christening -- these are parish records covering both, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So these figures here in this table do not deal only with Croats; there are Hungarians also in there, Hungarians who left. Now, where did they go, I don't know. Maybe you know. But as of now, we have not heard any Hungarians -- any Hungarian victims who would have told us anything here. I have no idea why these Hungarians would have left in the first place, but all I can do is draw a conclusion that now in table 9, we have not only Croats, but also Hungarians.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is correct, this is how the parish records were made, no distinction to ethnicity. But I suggest now we refer to page 30 of the report, table 17. In this table, the overall number of individuals listed in annex A of this report, 722, is shown by the country of destination. And for "to Croatia," as you see, it's the first category, there were 483 persons who left to Croatia. I don't see Hungarian on this list, but there is a category "unavailable," which is 233. Possibly there is Hungarians here. Who knows? But it is unquestionable that the major group of departing were the Croats, in the first place. Otherwise, why would Hungarians go to Croatia if they could go to Hungary next-door almost from Hrtkovci?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So table 17 on page 30 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Table 13 on page 30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- shows the out-migration from May to August 1992 and gives us absolute figures, right, this quantity? Is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This table shows the out-migration in 1992, not only May to August but also in other months in 1992, as presented in annex A, out-migration of 792 persons to certain destinations. Croatia is one of them, and it's the biggest one, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 483 go to Croatia; but out of these 483, there could be Hungarians, after all. They could benefit from the Geneva Convention, and they might have gone -- but they also might have gone to Hungary. We don't really know. Theoretically, it's possible that they could be included in this 483?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. They are not included in 483. This is the Croatian -- Croats, simply, who went to Croatia. Hungarians are not reported under 483.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What source did you use to find these 483 Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Basically, two sources. One was the refugee table sent to us by the Croat authorities. These are the records of refugees from Hrtkovci from Croatia, 116 people. Also there is the list of 280 families that was made by the VS-61. This list included the country of destination, and Croatia is recorded as the country of destination in this list. It is basically that the list and the parish records are one and the same source. It is VS-61 who registered, first of all, records in his administration; and at the same time, he compiled some kind of an overview of the departures, which is the list of 280. Whereas, in the parish records, there is no destination, there is no record of where they went to; in the summary of departures, there is a destination. For every family, we have information about where they went to. This is what is the basis for this table, and I think it is a good proxy, the destination, in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me take this opportunity to ask you another question that has to do with this table, but also that has to do with your report in general. Would you have drawn another conclusion out of these figures on Croats who left to Croatia, to go to Croatia? You're saying they are Croats because your sources are the refugee lists. Would you have maintained your conclusion had you known that one of these lists is a bit doubtful, in light of what we mentioned yesterday regarding, you know, the events around Mr. Grujic? Would you have drawn the same conclusions or not had you known that one of these sources was a bit doubtful?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I am not worried about Mr. Grujic at all because he's not the one who made this list. This list comes from an authority who is mandated to keep records of refugees. So that he requested the list from the appropriate ministry doesn't bother me, honestly, too much, because I know there is a serious group of people who take care of records of refugees in Croatia, and they do it in the right way. I had the opportunity to visit them, to meet with them. I was in the archive in which they keep the files. I saw how they computerised the records, how they make databases, and my impression of all this was that this was a professional group. This is one thing. That I obtained or we obtained the list in response to an RFA that was sent to Colonel Grujic is also not a big issue to me, because at the same time I have the source. I have the book, and from the book, I know who made the list. That is what matters. The actual source of the list is VS-61, and it is exactly the same source as for my parish records. I do have to trust my parish records because it is not a new thing in demography. It has a history of hundreds of years that these records are used in all kinds of studies, and produce reliable results. They are taken extremely seriously in demography. So I am still good, I feel, with my sources and my results. So that is how I feel about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a brief question, if I may. Could you please take a look at table 18 on page 31. It's on the page 31 in the English version, table 18. It would be nice to have the table on the screen. Now we have it. On the top table, there is a breakdown by age groups. Out of the 722 people, you have -- we have a distribution with age group and the sex also, men/women. Now, I'm going to look at the able-bodied men who were able to work, the category of people between 20 and 60, age 20 to 60. In that bracket, you know, you have 24 to 25 to 29 and all the way to 55, 59. So I will set aside the children, I'll set aside the seniors that are over 60. I'll only take adults, working adults, and only men, because in these type of migrations, usually it's men who take the decision and then they pack their belongings and wife and child, and everybody has to go. So if I sum up these men between 20 to 60, I see there are about 170 Croats that are in that bracket, 170 decision-makers, if I could call them so, who decided to pick up their belongings and go, taking with them maybe children and grandparents and so on. So this decision was made by 170 people. Do you see this is what happened? If I sum up your tables --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is a group of individuals for whom age is unknown; and for men, this group is 178. This is the last category reported in the table. So the 170 Your Honour just mentioned is a minimum number of decision-makers. But if we go to the table right next to this one, then we have the corrected numbers, and then the number will be bigger, if it's far more than 170. This makes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But in this very large migration of people going from Serbia to Croatia, at most here you have about 200 decision-makers who decided to pick up their stuff and go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would think about 280 because these are the families mentioned, and this is consistent more or less with this table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with you. Fine. Let's say 280, let's even say 300. There are 300 decision-makers who, for some kind of reason, decided to go. You agree with that, you agree with that figure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree, but we are speaking only about the year 1992, and actually a period, not the entire year, but a part of the period. It makes sense, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we are in 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This would be mainly Croats -- exclusively Croats, actually, this number, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Absolutely. I believe that we might have explored some different avenues, and I do remember that Mr. Seselj is cross-examining at the moment. So you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau, why did you not act as a conscientious and moral scientist, and why did you not, at the very beginning of the expert report, provide comparative data; ethnic composition of Croat, according to the census in 1991; the ethnic composition of Serbia or Vojvodina, according to the 1991 census, on the other side; then the ethnic structure of Croatia, according to the 2001 census; and then the ethnic structure of Vojvodina, according to the census of 2002? You say Vojvodina is a lot smaller than Croatia. What does that mean? Statistically, it means nothing. Vojvodina has a population of two million, Croatia about four and a half million. Don't correct me straight away with the absolutely exact figures. They don't matter at all. Croatia is two times bigger than Vojvodina, in terms of population numbers. So why did you not provide that? Your objective should be to come to the truth and to explain the process; whereas, you tendentiously falsify the process with inaccurate data outside any kind of serious context.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't see it necessary to include this particular comparison of the populations in Croatia and Vojvodina, as the focus of my report was just one village in Vojvodina. So I just didn't see it necessary. Moreover, I don't see this kind of work as a game of numbers. This is a wrong perspective. I think it is necessary to focus on a particular case and what actually can be shown in a justified manner for this particular place, and this is what I did to keep the discussion focused and relevant to this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You are talking about the broader context only when it supports your point of departure or your basic aim to justify the indictment; and if it doesn't suit your purposes, then you neglect the entire context; right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not true. I appreciate the importance of the broader context, but I do not like the game of numbers. This is one thing. The broader context, if we speak about really broad context, it's much broader than the two censuses for Croatia and Vojvodina, 1991 versus 2002. It is the numbers that need to be placed in a perspective, and the perspective is the broader socio-economic and political situation in the region. I didn't feel qualified to make any statements about these kind of broader contexts. I'm a demographer and not a politician or historian or economist. So this is a work, a project that is meant for a much broader group than just demographers, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Your expert report doesn't show that you're a serious demographer. The only thing I see is that you are a not very skilful manipulator. You say that you don't like the game of numbers, but that is exactly what you are doing by --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, do not say that Ms. Tabeau has been playing with numbers. She made a report. She was mandated and commissioned by the OTP to do so, and that's what she told us. Maybe the report could have been broader, more comprehensive, but she was commissioned to do a certain job and did that very job. I'm talking under her control, but I believe that if she had been given a broader topic to study, she would have studied a broader topic. But she was asked to do a very specific job that was focusing on a specific locality. Right, Ms. Tabeau, you had a specific job? You were commissioned by the OTP to do something, and you were not asked -- the OTP didn't ask you to do this or that, but gave you a job?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. This is what I said yesterday, and when we discussed causes of migration, I said I was not tasked to study the causes. My task was to describe out-migration, and this is what I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Proceed. Mr. Seselj, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you have statistical data about the population census dating to 1981 in Vojvodina?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have some published statistics, aggregate statistics. I didn't have the actual data, census data, in my office.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you have any information to this effect, that from the period from 1981 to 1991, Vojvodina had a negative balance of births; that is to say, that the population increase was negative and the white plague, as we called it, reigned with a negative balance of births?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suggest we refer to table 4 in my report. That actually is a review of the population growth in Vojvodina since 1948. This is a table that is based on published statistics on the population of Vojvodina, census statistics. I didn't make the table. I took it from a published source, which is mentioned under the table. It is page 15 in the report, page 15, table 4 in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Why aren't you giving me short answers to my short questions? My question was short. Your answer takes 15 minutes. Now, do you know that this negative balance was with 21.000 inhabitants between the 1981 and 1991 census - just say "yes" or "no" - in the whole of Vojvodina, almost 21.000 people?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what the table says, only that what you said about the natural increase, it was not negative. All the major components which was positive of the population growth was because of the natural increase, and the main factor contributing to the negative growth was the migration balance, and this is what this table says. So the population growth is a result of two factors: Natural population growth, which is the difference between the births and the deaths; and migration balance. According to the changes in these two factors, populations grow or decline. You are right, when saying that in 1981 to 1991, the overall growth was negative. So the population size dropped by approximately 21.000. That is very correct. This is what this table says, but the factor behind this drop is the migration balance. This what is shown in this table. The migration was negative, so people were leaving this province already in this decade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What was the reason for people leaving during that decade? It was still a period of communism between 1981 and 1991, so what was the exclusive reason for people's departure?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that you will tell me because it is not what I discussed in my report. I may think of all kinds of reasons. I may think of economic migration, educational migration, any kind of migration, but you probably have more specific information about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I haven't come here to teach you, Ms. Tabeau. You should have learnt those things a long time ago. You should have researched them and then, as an expert, explain them to me here because I'm a layman. I'm an amateur in the subject of demographer, so it's up to you to explain things to me and not the other way around. But, anyway, is it true that negative growth -- negative population growth was recorded in all national groups between 1981 and 1991 among the Serbs and Hungarians and Croats and Rumanians and Ruthenians and all the rest?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your literature from Serbia and Vojvodina explained this negative migration balance in the period up to 1991 as developmental migration, with temporary work abroad. So I think that is the explanation. People were leaving because they wanted a better life and more money, and this is why this was happening. That is how I -- how I can explain this. It is all in my report, so you can look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Those are basically unidentified sources because what we call the white plague is something that Vojvodina has confronted for decades, but that's not my main point. You're not answering my question, actually. Is it true and correct that the negative population growth is something that each national community in Vojvodina had in the period between 1981 and 1991? Just answer my question directly, "yes, it's true," "no, it's not." Why are you saying all these other stupid things?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the population growth was negative between 1981 and 1991, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was it negative growth in all the ethnic communities? You had the figures before and everything was published in detail. There's a big book about all that, the results of the population census taken in 1981. I would have it here before me had I not been restricted communication with my associates.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what was the distribution, ethnic distribution, of the population growth, so I can't say whether this growth --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. So you don't know.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: For ethnicities, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Don't swallow up all my time. Just say you don't know, that's honest, and we can move on. You've eaten up all my time. Anyway, do you know that the negative population growth is something that all national communities had in Vojvodina between 1991 and 2002, with the exception of Serb refugees, who settled there during that period of time, so Serbs, Hungarians, Croats, Rumanians, Ruthenians, and all the others? Do you know about that? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: So what kind of settlers are you speaking of; Kosovo Serbs, for instance?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm leaving to one side the Serbs who came from Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, and Kosovo. I'm just referring to the Serbs who lived there in 1991 in Vojvodina and all the others, all the other ethnic groups. They had a negative population growth from 1991 to 2002; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we still can refer to this table I have just used, that would be table 4; and, obviously, you are wrong. Between 1991 and 2002, the overall growth was positive, and this was thanks to the huge immigration, that means people arriving in Vojvodina. This is mentioned in this table, and the population growth --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, good heavens, what is all this that you're telling me? Listen to what I'm asking you. Don't mention immigration growth. We're talking about -- let's exclude immigration growth for the time being and imagine that nobody had come into Vojvodina in this period of 11 years to settle. Just the population who lived there in 1991, just take that. In 2002, there's a negative growth, both Serbs and Croats and Hungarians and Rumanians and Ruthenians. I'm asking you an extremely simple question, but you don't seem to understand me, or else you're pretending not to. I hope that's the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Tabeau, we're now dealing with extremely complex matters, and those of us who are not well versed in maps may find it difficult to understand what it's all about. Let's go back to the beginning and look at the table in your report at page 15. According to this table, there's no doubt that between 1981 and 1991, if we take the census into account, the number of inhabitants declined, the population declined, and the figure is 21.000 people. No one can deny this. What is the cause of this decline? You gave the answer to that question, and Mr. Seselj mentioned it as well. This is due to the departure of inhabitants from the area, probably for reasons related to employment, the communist regime at the time, the situation in Vojvodina. So people were leaving to find work somewhere else. This trend lasted for ten years. So this trend existed before, and it does not relate to Serbs who would later come to the area, but it relates to people in Vojvodina itself. So could this trend, this phenomenon, have continued in the period between 1991 and 2002, a trend that has nothing to do with the war, with the conflict, with increasing tensions, with the speech of the 6th of May, 1992, according to the Prosecution? So this phenomenon, this trend, didn't it also apply to the period between 1991 and 2002, and shouldn't, as a result, the figures, the statistics, be seen in a different light because of this so-called white plague that could have continued between 1991 and 2002? It's a phenomenon, it's a trend that has absolutely nothing to do with the events that took place in 1991 and 1992. What's your take on this, because I believe that's what Mr. Seselj is driving at. It may be a bit difficult to understand, but I, myself, understood that it was the precise question he was trying to ask you. So what do you have to say? Just one thing, if these events had not taken place, if Yugoslavia had remained as it was in the old system, then wouldn't the census of 2002 have registered a decline of the population anyway because people would have continued to leave to go to Canada, Germany, what have you? Did you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did. Thank you for the explanation. I believe there was an out-migration related to looking for a better life before the 1991 census, and this is expressed in table 4 by the negative migration balance. I believe that around 1990, 1991, the whole region was affected by dramatic events, by war in Croatia, Slovenia first. So this is a completely, total different situation which most certainly had impact on decisions, migratory decisions, of people. I believe - this is a belief; I didn't study it - that those who already were abroad, having jobs in, for instance, Western countries, might have decided to stay there and not to come back home in this period, as the times were not good for returning home; or perhaps on the contrary, perhaps they wanted to protect their property. Who knows? But I tend to believe the decisions would be just to stay. We are speaking about here, after the 1991 census, is a totally different situation, and this is expressed also in table 4 with data for 1991-2002. Everything changes in the period. Look at the rate of natural increase. People don't want to have children anymore because it is somehow too uncertain to decide to have a family in this period. There are -- the rate of natural increase is negative in this period, so that's an important difference between the previous period and this period. So I don't think that the assumption of a continuation of the developmental migration from before 1991 applies here. I don't think that, demographically speaking, we can just assume that it is just continuing and even more people are leaving because they want a better life. I don't think that the motivation for migration remains exactly the same in these two periods. It's unlikely it remains the same because the whole situation is upside down. It is a conflict going on there in these areas, so this changes people's perspectives on everything. I'm not sure I answered the question, but shortly I don't believe that developmental migration continued after 1991. It is a different form of migration that we have to think of. It is - I'm sorry to say this - it is forced migration. This is how we call it in demography, and this migration would cover, of course, refugees and would cover voluntary migration, "voluntary" in the sense that nobody expelled these people physically from their houses, but voluntary but war-related first. Migration, we have to think of this migration as a consequence of conflict as well. That is the motivation for people's decision in this period in the first place, I believe. So it's not that things weren't there before 1991. The situation has changed totally in the beginning of the 1990s, and so did the motivation for migration. This is what I think about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I believe that the witness has now answered your question. According to her, after 1991, the trend that existed before did not continue to apply.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I thought that she had answered. You don't share my view. Please try to establish that. But according to me, she's answered your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't receive the interpretation of those last words of yours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I was saying that I believe that she has answered by saying that the trend that took place between 1981 and 1991 did not continue to apply after 1991 because according to the witness, other motivations came into play, related, among other things, to the war, and that explained why people were leaving. The same -- the causes or the motivations of the previous period did not apply anymore. That's what I understood, and you may not agree with the witness. We may not agree with the witness, but that's what she answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau, instead of being a demographer and entering into research, you're being a philosopher and trying to think. Now, you think there are different reasons between 1991 and 2002, and not the economic reasons, prompting people to leave, but we had a blockade in Serbia, the Federal Republic of Serbia, a terrible economic blockade already in 1992, May 1992, in fact. That's when it started. Had it not been for intimations of that blocked, people were already leaving. Then at the end of the 1990s - I don't know what year it was exactly - Hungary became a member of the European Union, so the economic prosperity of Hungary. Under the blockade, there was no bread in Serbia, no employment, salaries were tantamount to just two German marks, whether you were working in the socialist sector or the private sector, or wherever. Your expert report shows none of that. Secondly, we have a negative growth for Ruthenians and Rumanians and Slovakians and Hungarians and everybody, except the Roma in Vojvodina. You had this data at your disposal. The Prosecution has the data at their disposal. So why are you inventing things and saying that those factors were not active in the 1990s, when there was social poverty, the main economic factor at the time?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may comment on this, please look at table 4 again. Why, then, is there a huge immigration in this period of the economically-poor development or non-development? There is a number of migration balance given in the table, and it is huge and positive. We all know these were mainly Serbs coming in, so they didn't care for the economic situation. For the fact that there was no bread, there were problems, everything was expensive, they were coming in. This is the proof that I'm right by saying that the motivation for the population movement in this period is not the same as before 1991. It is a different motivation and has to do with the conflict. It has to do with the conflict in Croatia, on the first place, also in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and in Kosovo after all as well later; right? But it is rather certain that you are not right by saying that they were -- that people were pushed out from Serbia and Montenegro and Vojvodina, as part of Serbia, by economic factors and pulled by a better life elsewhere. I would disagree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Because you did not approach this research seriously. Had you done that, you would have known what the total figure was of Serbs who moved out of Serbia in this period from 1992 until 2000, how many moved out to Canada, Australia, America, those who fled from poverty during those years of blockade, but you did not research that. You say -- or rather, you are refuting what I'm saying by the fact that enormous numbers of Serbs came in. Yes, Serbs came in, but they were saving their bear lives. They were fleeing from Croatia. They were expelled from Croatia. They were trying to save their very lives, and they fled even to an impoverished country. You, as a demographer, are not in a position to understand that because you're not a real demographer. You're just carrying out the instructions of the OTP in order to support a false indictment. That's the core of the matter. Secondly, in this table, you say that 81.000 people in Vojvodina is the number of people who died, and that more people died than were born, and that pertains to the entire population of Vojvodina. Don't go into the migrants now. You have the death rate and the birth date. The difference between the births and the deaths, natural deaths, is 81.171; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not wish to interrupt you, Mr. Seselj. I was waiting for you to finish, but I wanted to say that you surrendered based on the indictment, that was confirmed by the Judge, so you can't talk about a false indictment. You cannot use that sort of language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, apparently, at the time, the economic situation -- I say "apparently" because we don't have any evidence to that effect; Mr. Seselj is telling us that. But when somebody tells me something, I tend to trust him or her implicitly. So, at the time, there was an economic blockade, and Mr. Seselj is telling us that people would be paid about two Deutsche marks a month at the time. He also added something that we to not see in your report, and that Serbs - and here I'm not talking about Croats - but that Serbs, because of this situation, decided to leave, decided to go away from Vojvodina. They left. But we also know that other Serbs arrived in Vojvodina because there were refugees. And in the table we find, at page 10 of your report, we have the numbers of Serbs in Hrtkovci in 1991, from 531 in 1991 and 2.396 in 2002. We must remember that Serbs coming from Croatia or other places arrived. But notwithstanding that fact, there must have been Serbs who left the region during that period for economic reasons. Undeniably, some Serbs left. Can you agree with that? Can you agree that it may very well be that some Serbs left Hrtkovci, left Vojvodina, for reasons linked to the blockade, because they were only paid two Deutsche marks a month and they decided to go somewhere else where they would earn much more money? Would we be mistaken to take that factor into account?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First, a general comment. Every migration decision is a result of a complex net of factors. There are generally two groups of these factors, pull and push factors, and the interplay between these two groups of factors is the result of migratory decisions. Normally, in peace, the pull factors play a very important role. The grass is greener, of course, elsewhere. This is basically how it is. But in politically-unstable times, in conflict situations, these are the push factors that play a role in the first place. Although I haven't done, myself, research on this, these are well-known facts in demography. If you wish, I can look for publications and bring you papers, and this can be discussed in a more justified -- scientifically-justified manner. Well, of course, regarding the specific question, of course I am not saying that no Serb left because the economic situation was so bad, but the situation in this period cannot be seen exclusively as economic because this was the political situation that was together with the economic situation. That must be seen as the push factors. At the same time, if people had some opportunities anywhere to go, then the strong push factors and these opportunities there were resulting in certain decisions. So I'm not saying that Serbs all stayed and Croats all have gone. That is very incorrect. This is not what I'm saying, because the real life is never black and white. There were cases of Serbs who migrated because of the bad economic situation, but at the same time as the bad political situation, of tensions, of intensifying ethnic conflict, and et cetera, et cetera. I didn't study these, but I'm sure that there were other witnesses who are speaking about these general factors. So this is all I am saying. I hope that is all. But regarding the question you asked me, first of all, there was a specific question about the natural increase between 1991 and 2002. Yes, it was negative, and the number is in table 4 on page 15. Actually, I already answered the question related to the out-migration of Serbs from Serbia. I don't exclude it as a fact, but I didn't study it and I do not have figures of that in my report. I'm pretty sure there are publications on this, and, again, I can look for these publications. There will be articles produced in Yugoslav survey and other authors. If Your Honours wish to see these kind of publications, again, to avoid speculation and to have figures, I would be most happy to find these publications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's 10.00. We need to break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Court is back in session. Mr. Seselj, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau, how do you explain the fact that from 1991 until 2002, the population of the Slovak ethnic minority went down by 11 per cent?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't explain this in the report, and I'm not explaining this now as well. I would need to study it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you have information to the effect that 10.9 per cent was the decline in the Slovak ethnic minority population?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, as I said, I didn't study it and I don't want to speculate about it. So I can't confirm or approve or disapprove the number you are giving me accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this document be put on the ELMO? The 65 ter document number is 02754.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How come you work at the OTP and don't know about this document? That's a shameful thing, and we got that document along with the set for this witness. Do we have it on the ELMO now? Right. Not yet? We have the first page. Please, let's see the second page. This is information on trends --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note; it's too fast for interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: See, according to the census of 2002, in Vojvodina there is 56.000 Slovaks; and in 1991, there was 63.545. At the end of the first paragraph, it says that the number went down by 6.908, or rather, 10.9 per cent. You never had this document in your hands?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't say I did not receive information, census data, from the 2002 census on several minority groups in Vojvodina. I didn't say this. I said I didn't study this. The focus of my report was on Croats, mainly, and Hungarians as the representatives of the non-Serbs in Vojvodina and Hrtkovci, on the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: However, when you make such far-reaching conclusions as far as Croats are concerned, why didn't you compare the situation regarding the Croat ethnic minority with the Slovak, Romanian, Ruthenian, and other minorities? Wouldn't a conscientious scholar do that straight away? If a conscientious scholar were to see that there was a reduction of 11 per cent in the number of Slovaks, and what was the decline in the number of Croats, about 20 per cent? So Slovaks, 11 per cent less. Do you know that Slovaks live in compact communities in Vojvodina, in Backi Petrovac, Kovin, Stara Pazova, Borci? Don't you know that?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: One correction to the transcript, line 17: "I didn't say I did receive," instead, this is how the transcript should read in this line, line 17: "I didn't say I did not receive..." I did receive the data on the 2002 census.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You have no explanation?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was going to come to my answer to your question. It is in my report that all these other minorities are shown in table 2 for Vojvodina, and we can refer to this table jointly as the so-called "others." So what I really didn't do is I didn't separate every single minority group, as I did with Croats and Hungarians, because the other groups are shown jointly as "others."

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. That's not an answer to my question. Do you have an explanation as to how come the number of Hungarians went down by 15 per cent? Were the Hungarians persecuted, expelled? You don't know. Okay. Let's move on --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. I have an answer. I don't see the 15 per cent decline for Hungarians in my table for Vojvodina. This is one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Could I have 02757, that's the 65 ter number, and then I will show you. It seems that I have better glasses than you do. The OTP provided me with all this information. It would have been better had I been the Prosecution expert witness for demography. Could we have the document, and could Ms. Biersay not get up because we are moving on to the core of the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Look at the second paragraph. The Hungarians went down by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Biersay, you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I am on my feet to remind Mr. Seselj that these sources are listed in Dr. Tabeau's report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Tabeau obviously has not mastered this and has not used this information. Had she responded to me that she was aware of this information, I wouldn't have to use this document. Now, this is the document that she allegedly relies on in her report and that the OTP provided to me, and that is the number of Hungarians went down by 49.284 persons, or rather, 15 per cent. I have to move on now, because I don't have too much time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau, how do you explain the fact that the Romanian ethnic minority population in Vojvodina went down by 21.6 per cent from 1991 until 2002?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I would prefer that Mr. Seselj makes exact reference to the material that he's discussing. It was part of the court binder prepared for this testimony, that the sources I used in the report are attached in this binder. So if we could have the translation of the Serbian text which is on the screen, so that we could directly confirm the numbers. But as far as I can see from my data in the report that are coming from the specific data from the sources attached to the court binder, we could at least have some idea that the numbers he's referring to are correct. But without checking this, it's hard to have any discussion of these numbers at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Tabeau is already playing the role of Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please slow down. The interpreter cannot follow this at this speed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Tabeau, we have a document that comes from the OTP. This document was sent to Mr. Seselj. I assume that you also obtained this document; you also probably obtained it. It would be quite incredible if you hadn't seen this document. It's a document that's new to me, as far as I'm concerned, but it doesn't take me hours to understand a document. It does seem to be an official document, and it says that the number of Hungarians had dropped by 15 per cent in Vojvodina between 1991 and 2002. Do you agree with it, you don't agree with it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I am aware of these documents. These were some data tables sent to us from the Office for Minorities in Vojvodina with the summary text here that is on the screen related to the Hungarians minority. There were data tables. As part of these data tables, statistics were presented, based on census, for settlement. These statistics have been processed and are presented in my report. This is table 2 for Vojvodina, as a whole, and table 1 for Hrtkovci. So it is not true that I didn't use this particular data. I did use relevant parts of the data in my report. And if I would have looked at every minority separately, my report would be much bigger than what it is now. The focus of the report, as I am saying, is mainly Croats, so this is the reason that I'm not referring to every single minority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But, generally speaking, if it appears that there was a decline for all minorities, all of them, one could infer from this that the phenomenon that affects minorities also affected the Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it is how it is, yes. So I never said that the only group that was affected were the Croats, not even one time in my report. So I don't -- I'm missing the point here, but, okay, perhaps it will be coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And how were you able to establish the demographic situation of the national community of Croats in Vojvodina without making a comparative analysis with the situation of the other national minorities, ethnicities? How can any scientist or person engaged in scholarly investigation omit to do that?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't take the analysis of Croats out of context because the tables which we have been discussing, table 1 and 2, is not -- are not made for exclusively Croats. All ethnic groups are there in the tables, sir, and the entire population of, in table 1, Hrtkovci and Vojvodina are shown. The issue is that you are telling me that I should have shown every minority separately. Yes, this could have been done. I didn't do it for simplicity. This is why the tables are as they are. But all minorities are included in the tables. They are not excluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes. But your simplifications were in the function of falsifying scientific data and evidence because scientific evidence would have been quite different had you conducted a comparative analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me have the 65 ter document -- 02753 is the number, page 2. Page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Can you see there that the number of citizens of Romanian ethnicity was reduced by 21.6 per cent in Vojvodina in the period during the two censuses, and the number of Croats fell by 24 per cent? Can you see that, Ms. Tabeau? Would you like to have my glasses, if you can't see?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mine are very good. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I'm waiting for your answer a long time. Can you see it or not? It's the first paragraph, and I would have read through it 15 times already. Do you know, Ms. Tabeau, that never through history, throughout history, there were never any conflicts between the Serbian and Romanian people and that Serbia and Romania never went to war against each other? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. But don't ask me questions about history. But the thing is, Mr. Seselj, that the population of Romanians, if you look into the text, is very small compared with the population of Hungarians and the population of Croats. So my selection of ethnic groups, like Croats and Hungarians, first of all, were related to the population of these groups in the population of Vojvodina. It doesn't make really much sense to speak about every single minority if the minority group is of the size of 3.000, 2.000, 5.000, in the population of two million. You are referring to percentages that are related to this size of populations, so that is the misleading part on your side, not on my side, because my decision is justified by the size of the minority populations that I took for my report. This is not a matter of bad glasses. This is a matter of, you know, how you read the numbers that are on this page. You really need to think a little bit what you are reading on paper. It's a matter of interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau, don't falsify things here on the spot. We're not talking about 5 or 6.000 Romanians, but Romanians, according to the 1991 census, there were 38.809, which is just half the number of Croats. So don't underestimate these statistical samples because here we see a trend emerging which was present with the Serbs in Vojvodina, with the exclusion of Serb refugees who have arrived in recent years.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now let's take a look at what the situation is like with the Ruthenians, and that is 02758 under 65 ter. That's the document number.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may comment on the size of minorities, if you look at my table, the number Croats and Hungarians, in 1991, is about 400.000; whereas, the number of all others, other ethnic groups jointly, including the groups you just discussed, is 268.000, approximately. So, even though the size of this population was about 30.000, we are still speaking of minorities that are far smaller than Croats and Hungarians jointly. So that is my point, and I will defend my tables in the report the way they have been done because that is the right way to do it. It is often done in statistics that distributions are presented for aggregate ethnic groups in which minorities of a smaller size are shown together.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And according to what methodological procedure did you link up the Hungarians and Croats, when it's common knowledge that between those two nations for centuries there has been a national tension, that is to say, that they, Serbs and Hungarians, got on much better than the Croats and Hungarians? There was animosity between them, so how do you listening them up to make the number larger? Look at the 1991 census and tell us how many Croats there were.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't link Croats and Hungarians, and I don't know about the relationship between these groups and the Serbs, not the relationship at present, not the relationship in the past. I just don't know about it, and, you know, I don't know. For the second part of the question, the size of the Croat population is about 72.000, 72 or 73.000 in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Take a look at the figure for the Ruthenians, 11.5 per cent less Ruthenians. Quite opposed to what you said a moment ago, the fewer numbers of the national minority, the lower the decrease. There was just 17.652 Ruthenians. Now there are 15.626. So the reduction was just 11.5 per cent; whereas, where there were larger ethnic minorities, like the Slovaks and Romanians, the decrease in percentages is far greater. That is -- absolutely goes against the grain of what you said a moment ago, 11 and a half per cent less Ruthenians.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now let's have a look at the next document. 02758 is the number -- no, 02755 is the document I'd like pulled up on e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may comment. Relating the size of the change with the size of the ethnic group, the bigger the group, the bigger the change, doesn't make sense, really. So I definitely disagree with what you said. That is --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: No. You don't agree with yourself because a moment ago you advocated this thesis: If the number was too few of the members of a certain ethnic minority, then the percentages of decrease is higher. Now, let's look at the figures which relate to the Roma. Where the Roma are concerned, we have an increase of 19 per cent. How do you explain that? All the national minorities or ethnicities are declining; whereas, the Roma, who are all over Europe, increase as a population to the tune of 19 per cent. Do you have an explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. But if you look in table 2, then you will see that all other minorities, except for Croats and Hungarians, the size of the population of all other minorities between 1991 and 2002 increased. So is it so surprising that Roma are shown here as an increased population between the two censuses?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, that explanation merits being recorded in an encyclopedia. Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Tabeau, I'm a bit lost with your answer here. You said -- you did indicate that in the category called "Others," and we see this on the table, table 2, we see that between 1991 and 2002, there was an increase for "Others." So in these "Others," 268.294 for 1991, and in 2002, 313.551. So at least 50.000 people more called "Others," who came from or who arrives from God knows where. Now, regarding this category called "Others," you might have been more specific here because we find other minorities. That's what we're finding out, that there are others included in this "Other." Some minorities are down by 10, 15, 20 per cent, and there's one minority that's on the increase, the Romas, and we have no idea why. They should also be declining, but they are increasing. There's probably some logical explanation, but we don't have it. There must be an explanation for this. So, if there's a general trend, when there's a trend - that's a technical term, this trend - so when there's a general trend and if this general trend impacts all minorities, including the Croats, who are also a minority, shouldn't the reason that causes this decline in all minorities, except for the Romas, don't you think you should have identified this cause?
