Did you tell yourself, "Oh, minorities are on the decline. Why is it? Is it why the number of Croats also declined or is there a specific reason that would have to do with persecutions?" Because that's the whole topic, in fact. I'm sure you understood this. The Judges here will have to decide whether the Croats who are in your chart left because of the consequences of harassment, intimidation, speeches, and so on, whether they left because of this or whether they left for different motivations, for different reasons. We're going to have to decide on that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There is a number of minorities in Vojvodina, Croats and Hungarians being the largest of them. The decline in the population size of minorities is seen, and not only for Croats and Hungarians, but also for other minorities, with the exception of, for instance, Roma. I don't remember but there were perhaps other minorities that increased slightly in this period as well; but, generally, there is a decline in minority populations in Vojvodina between these two years, 1991 and 2002. I don't like using the table, presenting summary terms of statistics to discuss these kind of issues, because the statistics for 2002 are not directly comparable with statistics for 1991. That is one thing. So the increase in the group called, in my table, "Others," I believe is partly because of changing ethnicity reports in the 2002 census. There is my theory - it is not that I studied this with empirical data - which is that some of the Yugoslavs perhaps are here in this group. Perhaps. Who knows? Perhaps some of them have become Serbs in the time between 1991 and 2002. So it is not a good basis, the census figures, aggregate statistics, for this kind of discussion. This is what Mr. Seselj is doing, using aggregate statistics and discussing the declines or increases by looking at aggregate statistics. So what is really important, in my view, are additional data that are in the report and relate to the Croats and Hungarians that give our -- give us more insight into about what was happening in this time. In my view, there is no doubt about the fact that there were departures of Croats, on the first place, in this period in 1992 from Hrtkovci, and Vojvodina in general; and these kind of conclusions are also to be found in the very same minority reports that are discussed now. So if we go to the section about Croats, which is not shown right now on the screen, there will be passages about why the decline of Croats had taken place in this period. This is not that I wrote the passages. It is that the authorities, the minority authority, wrote this passage. There is a clear reference to the persecution of Croats in the period already starting in 1991, and I'm quoting in my report two passages from this report, minority report, which are on page 14.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's all move to page 14, then. What paragraph are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... paragraph from the bottom in italics, beginning with: "A major decline in the number of Croats ..." If I may read further: "A major decline in the number of Croats in the AP Vojvodina, in relation to the 1991 census, is evident in all the municipalities where a significant number of members of this minority used to live. This drop is seen as a consequence of the 1991 war in the immediate neighbourhood and, related to it, certain political forces at the time which were heavily engaged in expelling the Croatian population, especially in those populated places where they comprised a prominent or relative majority of the population or represented a significant percentage." So Hrtkovci is obviously such a place. The Croats are 40 per cent in 1991, and they are not an absolute majority, but they are a majority, a relative majority, in the village. The next paragraph, coming from the same source, the 2003 minorities report prepared in Vojvodina by the minorities authority in Vojvodina. I didn't write it: "The biggest decline in the Croatian population, which was mostly the result of a policy of persecution of the Croatian population during the years of the war in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, especially in 1991 at the time of the war operations in the territory of the Republic of Croatia, occurred," this decline, the biggest decline, "occurred in the in the municipality of Sid. Sid's Croatian population fell to only a third of that in the previous census," previous is 1991, and the current census is 2002," that is, from 6.047 to 2.086, or, expressed in percentages, a drop of 65.50 per cent. It is followed by the municipality of Indjija, with 59.05 per cent; Ruma," where Hrtkovci is located, "with 47.85 per cent ..." and so on and so on. A number of municipalities are mentioned with the percentage change, the decline in the Croat population. In reference to Hrtkovci, to the Croat population of Hrtkovci, the decline is about, as far as I'm correct, 67 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This text that you have just read out, we need this for the transcript. Could you tell us exactly what source it comes from? Who actually drafted this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The source is mentioned on page 2 of my report, page 2 English version. The report is the last item listed on the page. The title is "On the fluctuation in the number on Croatian ethnic minority in the AP Vojvodina, 1992-2002," and the source is the Provincial Secretariat for Regulations Administration and National Minorities in Novi Sad, Vojvodina. The report is dated 20 September 2003, and similar reports, I'm saying in the same paragraph, for other minority groups are available as well. This is what Mr. Seselj was discussing, for Hungarians, Slovaks, Romanians, Romas, Ruthenians. So that's the source for these two passages that are referred to in my, report and the source for the figures that we've been discussing most recently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So this is an official report. It's a Serbian official report, not Croatian. This comes from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And it's the same source as what was shown on the screen earlier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Proceed, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In dealing in demographic research, you are looking for political comments from people who are akin to you, from a moral and political point of view. What does this political explanation have to do with the information provided here? Where is proof for this thesis? In 2003, Nenad Canak is in power in Vojvodina, and Nenad Canak is the spitting image of the OTP, ideological and politically. So what does that have to do with your research, this quotation? What are you proving with this, that political players are providing this kind of explanation; nothing else?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the person you mentioned, and it's not true that I'm engaging in a discussion of politics in my report. A minority report that is discussed in my report was, for me, first of all, the source for the data which I use for Hrtkovci in my study. That is the most important part of it. Secondly, there is a commentary to the data provided. So that's all I can say. I was just reading the commentary and choosing the data, and this has nothing to do with the person who was in charge in Vojvodina of any political or other structures. There is an authority who's responsible for monitoring the situation of minorities in Vojvodina, and that's the institute, and that's the people who send me the data. So that is the end of story. Again, I have no reason to distrust this group of people and distrust the data. I compared the data with other published sources related to the census 2002, and there were no discrepancies, so I didn't have any reasons to reject the data and the source, as such. That's all I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Statistical data is one thing that you use, as a demographer, and political comments that you accept and quote are a different matter. As for this political comment, it simply should not be in your expert report, because for you to make this kind of a comment, it has to be supported by the data provided in your expert report. However, on the basis of the data you have available, you cannot come to this kind of an explicit conclusion and then it's much easier for you to take over, at face value, the political conclusion of some organ and you quote that; right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree. In the very same passages, especially the second one, there is an overview of changes in a number of municipalities, Ruma being one of them, and this is very relevant, in a statistical context, for the figures in this report. I don't believe I'm making any political statement in my report. I am just quoting from an authority mandated to monitor the minorities, and they are trying to explain the change. That's all. There is nothing about politics and me being involved in making political, yeah, statements; not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's have this table number 1; that is, 0289F. That's the 65 ter number. It has to do with Hrtkovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When you were given this project, this assignment to deal with the situation in Hrtkovci, you bore in mind the fact that this is a small village with a population of only 2.500; right? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You know that statistics is a science of big numbers. Statistical methods can lead to reliable information only when big groups are compared. When there are small groups, small sets, the statistical approach becomes unreliable. The smaller the numbers, the less reliable the outcome. Therefore, it has to be submitted to different kinds of checks; right? Am I right, as a layperson, when I say this in respect of statistical methods?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when it comes to estimating things, then of course statistics is a science of big numbers, big samples, strictly speaking. But statistics is much more than that. We are speaking here about observed numbers. At least in my report, this is the main part of the report, the observed numbers. The data I present, the list of 722, is a minimum number, the minimum number that can be documented with names other information about individuals. The statistics of big numbers and big samples has nothing to do with that, so you are mixing up things. So your comment was almost good, but not necessarily good in regard to my report; not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: From a demographic point of view, you just have two reliable sources, relatively reliable, like aid source, but those are your most reliable sources; that is, the census of 1991 and the census of 2002. A few moments ago you mentioned something which is the greatest nonsense you've uttered altogether, that the census of 2002 cannot be compared to the census of 1991; whereas, from a statistical point of view, that is the only measurable thing. That is the only thing that can be compared; right? Now, since you have been given the assignment to deal with a village that had a population of 2.528 inhabitants, instead of seeking invalid sources, as you did in relation to that priestly book and whatever else you looked at, you should have gone into the database of the republican statistics office of Serbia, and you should have studied there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, Ms. Biersay is on her feet. Let's see what she has to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I originally got up because Mr. Seselj asked a question, said, "right," and continued into yet a second question. So that was my original purpose for standing up. Now I'd like to request a redaction to page 54, line 9, for the reasons that we previously discussed in private session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. No, it cannot be deleted. I'm referring to Marko Kljajic's book when I say "priestly book." That is a book that was published in Serbia that was offered into evidence here. That cannot be deleted, the priestly book of Marko Kljajic published for propaganda purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Biersay, the book written by this priest was published. Everybody is aware of that book. Why would you want that line to be redacted where that book is mentioned, because everybody is aware of that book?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I think the reference was ambiguous, and I now wonder if the explication also creates a problem. But it was not clear to me what he was referring to. As the Court's aware, we have certain bits of evidence that could be characterized as books.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me confer with my fellow Judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After considering the matter, the Trial Chamber decides to keep the transcript as it is, without any redactions. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'll repeat that question for you, Ms. Tabeau. When you were given this project of dealing with a small village, the most natural thing to do was, from the very outset, to go into the database of the republican statistics office of Serbia and to have before you all the census documents for this village, because this is 2.528 forms. Wasn't that the most natural thing to do?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, most certainly, and this is what I did. I'm glad that you are saying this. We made an RFA to the authorities of Serbia and requested individual census records from Vojvodina. I would most certainly could then look at the 2.528 forms, but I never received this data because the data, I was told by the Serb statistical authority, was confidential, and that was the reason why not. So your point is totally invalid. This is what I wanted to see as an ideal approach, and it did not work out because data was not provided to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When was the last time that you asked for this officially?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me check, Mr. Seselj. It was in October 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: From October 2004 until October 2008, you did not even try to get this information, for all of four years. In the meantime, the Serb authorities sent Radovan Karadzic here. They disclosed to The Hague OTP all political -- police files, irrespective of the person that they pertain to. It is pointless to object here, because what I'm doing here is challenging the witness's methodological approach. For fours years, the expert witness did not deem it necessary to seek this information, and it's not secret information. It is not secret when it is used for judicial purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj -- or rather, Ms. Tabeau, there is a question I wanted to ask you yesterday. I didn't do so, but now I have the opportunity to put that question to you. Yesterday, you explained at length that you worked on the basis of resources, including the parish registers, and there's nothing to object to that. But I was wondering if there wasn't a fourth source that you may not have considered, i.e., the registers of the municipality of Hrtkovci. What prevented you from writing a letter to the persons in charge, to the municipality, to ask for copies of these registers, of these records? There was no need to wait for Serbia to cooperate fully. You could have done that before. Why didn't you request these records from the municipality, registers of births and deaths of the municipality? You could have gone there yourself to have a look at these records? Why didn't you do it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The municipalities have the so-called vital events registration. The vital events registration covers births and deaths, on the first place, and they also register marriages. Migration is not registered. Migration is not registered in the inter-census period. The only way to make an assessment of migration is to work with individual records from two censuses, compare them, and identify the number of people not reported in the later census. Having this done, it is then, in the next step, to look for these people who are missing, say, "missing," in the census records, using sources on displaced population and refugees. This was my initial plan, this is what I found the optimal approach, and this was not feasible. I must stress I have made many efforts to obtain the data that I needed for this project. That was not possible for me to work with the optimal data, and I believe the data used instead, parish records, there's nothing wrong with them. This is a very good source of information on, as well, migration; not only births and christenings and marriages, but also migration because the record of migration is taken in the parish books. The same with refugees, it's a very relevant source. Yes. So that is what is my answer to this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But couldn't you have used another source? I'm not sure, my question may not be relevant, but I suppose that these people at the time, the Croats, the Serbs, the Hungarians, and members of minorities, these people may have paid taxes, local taxes or what have you, but it would be surprising if this had not been recorded somewhere, everything related to taxes, to the payment of taxes by the population. Did you reflect on that? Did you wonder maybe if in 1991 the Croats were paying taxes, but not in 2002; in other words, they had left in the meantime? Did you consider that possibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't think about taxes. Well, it's unlikely that I would be given access to the tax records in Vojvodina and Serbia. It's very questionable. It's even more unlikely than receiving the census records, as the information contained in tax records is far more sensitive, of course. What I would need would be a full record of information with names of the individuals, addresses, and the tax record. So that is a lot of information. I'm really very skeptical about obtaining this source. I don't think there are sources that report on migration. Migration is known in demography to be the phenomenon that is most difficult from the point of view of sources. It's very hard to study migration, even in normal times, because migration is simply not systematically registered; and people who move don't automatically, after having moved, go and register themselves as migrants in a new country or in a new territory. So that is a very complicated phenomenon to study. This is part of my decision why I used the parish records.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I fully agree with you. But if you had 280 families paying taxes in 1991, and if in 1992 and 1993 they don't pay any taxes anymore, this may be evidence that they have left, indeed, because they are not paying any taxes. But I don't know anything about the tax system in the region, so my question or my comment may not be relevant. But this may be an avenue to explore to identify these people, because in legal proceedings, in judicial proceedings, that's a solution you can use to find people who have disappeared, provided, of course, that these people paid taxes. Because if they don't pay any tax, then it's completely irrelevant, although they might be recorded as not paying any taxes. But, in any case, it's something you did not actually consider?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. One thing was what I said. Another thing, it is not only important to know that people left, so that means stopped paying taxes at some point. It's important to know when they left, and that was one of the major issues, the timing of departures. And from this point of view, I wouldn't expect that the tax register would provide me with this information. So from this point of view, it is really useless. That people left, a group of people of Croat ethnicity, is rather obvious. I also used the census comparison, knowing even that there are certain biases, but thank God they don't apply to the Croat population to the extent that they apply to the population of Yugoslavs and others. Croat population is unbiased by trends in the perceptions of ethnicities, in my view, relatively, compared with other groups. The same with Serbs, the same is with Hungarians. So, for these three groups, I have relatively good comparison based on the census data. So there is no doubt there were departures from the village. The question was when these departures were taking place, and this is why parish records is an excellent source to study this as a source recording on the decisions they made, you know, to go and ask for the request. The decision, as such, as we discussed, is not the departure date, in itself; however, it is a decision, and this is what really matters. People were getting ready to leave, to take off, to go away from there; and that is, as such, it is an excellent measure of these decisions. And from this point of view, this is an important piece of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau, do you know that on the population -- in the population census in 1991 and the census in Serbia in 2002, the people conducting the census introduced a personal ID number for each citizen? Do you know about that, that the people conducting the census did that?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're speaking of the JMBG, then the number was introduced even earlier. It was in 1981 [Realtime transcript read in error "1991"]. The JMBG is the personal identification number. It was "1981," not "1991." I'm referring to the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, this is just terrible. I'm asking you about 1991 and 2002. I'm not interested in anything before that. What do I care about 1981? I'm asking you whether you know that on the basis of the JMBG number, the personal ID number, you can look up the register and see the name of the person listed. Is that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the 1991 and 2002 censuses, most certainly the JMBG is used. It's associated with individuals, so there's a name and date of birth and address and a lot of other data items associated with this -- through this number.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Therefore, there was no need for a lengthy answer like that, but you can follow the names. It is possible to follow the names from the 1991 census to the 2002 census. You can look at the names of each and every citizen. You can follow them. So if in 2002 there is a name missing, you can search for that name. You can search other sources to see where the person went. You can look at the death registers, if the person died; in the residence registrar, if he's changed addresses; and so on and so forth. Just say am I right or not with a yes-or-no answer, please.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well. Now, do you know who Dr. Svetlana Radovanovic is?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. How could I not know who Dr. Svetlana Radovanovic is. She has done a lot of work as a Defence expert in relation to my reports in other cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes. Now, my legal advisors engaged Dr. Svetlana Radovanovic, professor at the Faculty of Geography at the University in Belgrade to compile a report which will highlight the deficiencies of your expert report. Dr. Svetlana Radovanovic did indeed compile that report. Unfortunately, she wasn't able to hand it over to me, so I have not received it because all communication with my associates were severed, but I did arrive at some data and information that she had come by before the report was completed. Dr. Svetlana Radovanovic analysed all the 2.538 census forms of 1991, and all 3.428 census forms dating to 2002. That is part of the databases of the Republican Institute for Statistics, and via internet you can tap into that database. Unfortunately, after 2004, you didn't try to tap into that database, as you told us yourself. Now, in the vast number of pieces of information that Svetlana Radovanovic managed to come by, I find the most interesting the following: The one about how the citizens, the locals of Hrtkovci, declared themselves ethnically. I'll give you a few examples, you can make a note of them, and you can check them out during the next break to see whether or not that is true or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, please slow down when you give these numbers, because the interpreters don't have time to translate what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you don't have to interpret figures. That's not difficult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would really appreciate if this report or just pieces of the results from this report be distributed among all us in this courtroom, and to me in particular. As from the experience, I know the work of the professor, as you said, Professor Svetlana Radovanovic. It is not that her reports are completely error free and unbiased, and we can take these all for granted. So before I am even able to think whether this result makes sense or not, I definitely would like to see the results on paper. And regarding this particular example that Mr. Seselj started to discuss about changing the perception of ethnicity, this is not in contradiction with what was discussed earlier today.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: First of all, I can't access Dr. Svetlana Radovanovic's report myself because all contact with my associates has been severed. I would be happiest had those associates been able to supply me with that report on time so that I could hand it over to you, so that you could have it, the Prosecution could have it, and the Trial Chamber could have it. I would have done my job, because I'm a layperson with respect to demography, if compared to the important name that Dr. Svetlana Radovanovic undoubtedly is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, I know why you are on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The Prosecution objects to the mis-information that the accused continues to put on the record, that his communications with his associates have been severed, and we will object each and every time he says that. It's not true. It's a story that he's perpetrating and propagating through the Serbia media. It is simply not true, as this Chamber has told him repeatedly. We will object from this point forward each and every time Mr. Seselj says that his communications have been cut off, or his phones have been tapped, or that we're monitoring -- or the OTP is monitoring phone lines. We will object. So I'm simply telling him at this point that he can expect an objection, there will be objections, and we are not prepared to allow him to continue his campaign of mis-information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, we've already dealt with this issue at length, and we have once again to revisit the matter. The Chamber has already said it before. Communications are, indeed, monitored by the Registry. The Trial Chamber has received your oral motion, and I hope that we'll be able to rule on this motion very soon. But having said that, communications have not been severed. Mr. Mundis is right. Your communications are monitored. So there's nothing in the world that prevents you from receiving any type of report from your associates. That's the truth. But what happens is that you, yourself, have decided not to receive anything anymore from them. That's your choice, and we have nothing to say about this. But you have to tell things as they are. Yes, indeed, your communications are being monitored, but it is not true to say that you are being -- you're prohibited from doing so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. I'll give you the floor after making a few comments for Ms. Tabeau. Ms. Tabeau, you were saying that you would like to have such-and-such documents. Let me explain something. The burden of proof does not lie with Mr. Seselj, but with the Prosecution. In other words, Mr. Seselj does not have to produce all the exculpatory documents. He is entitled to put questions to you. I don't know this report that was mentioned. I know of this lady. Mr. Seselj may decide to call her as a Defence witness. I don't know. But if that's the case, then we can see what this person has to say. But the discussion here seems to be about the following: I, myself, asked you this morning, "Is it possible for people to declare themselves as Serbs during one census and as Croats at the following census," and you said, "Yes." Mr. Seselj has just established this with the examples of several individuals based on their personal identification numbers; therefore, there's no surprise here, because I asked you the question this morning myself and you said it was possible. Mr. Seselj, what did you want to say?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In prison, there are two telephones in each of the blocks. One telephone is a public telephone booth, which all the inmates use to ring up their friends, family, or whoever they want, and they pay for those phone calls. There's always a queue there because there are 11 of us on the floor. During the day, we have other things to do. We're locked up for two hours, then we have sports sessions, walks, and so on. Then there's another telephone which is used to contact legal advisers, associates, Defence counsel, and so on, and that is free of charge. By written order, I have not been allowed to use that telephone, and I can only use the public booth where there's always a long queue, and also I have to pay for my phone calls, which is not a negligible piece of information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I'm discovering this, and so is Mr. Mundis. Up until now, my fellow Judges, myself, and maybe Mr. Mundis, knew that this phone that was connecting you with your associates was being tapped, but now you're telling us that it's just you've been banned from using it. This is news to us, at least it is news to me. I know nothing about this. I'm sure Mr. Mundis knew nothing about it either.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was forbidden, in written form, in writing, to use that telephone; and from the list of privileged communications, the number of my legal adviser, Slavko Jurkovic was stricken from the list. As opposed to the other inmates, through this telephone, I was able to call up just one number, the number of Slavko Jurkovic. I couldn't dial any of the other case managers or legal advisors, just Slavko Jurkovic. The other number was the number of the Serbian embassy in The Hague. So just those two numbers, it was only those two numbers that I was able to dial from that particular telephone, not from the public booth. I can ring up any number. Not only will I be listened into by the Registry, but every other inmate waiting in the line, queueing up to telephone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you can use the public phone. We understand that you have to queue. It's unpleasant. We understand. But I'm absolutely flabbergasted by this. The phone that was tapped is a phone that you can no longer use through a written order; is that what you're telling us? Can you confirm this? We're going to ask the Registry about this. This is an infringement of your rights. Up until now, what we knew was that you could have a privileged line as long as you only used it to prepare your case. The Registrar decided that he needed to monitor what you were doing. That's his responsibility and the President's responsibility, and the Trial Chamber has been seized with your oral motion. But that's where we stood up until now. We did not know that you were banned from using this phone through a written order. But you confirm this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The Registry made a written decision to intercept my conversations with my legal advisers, and the warden issued a written order by which I was banned from using that number anymore. I can only call the Serbian Embassy, or rather, the consulate, Kljajic, and nobody else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will inquire with the Registry. I'm absolutely, really surprised. It looks like an invisible hand to doing its best to slow things down, to slow this trial down, and to prevent us from doing our job, because with this, I mean, you complain, and then we have objections from the Prosecution, the Trial Chamber has to rule on this. It's a waste of time. My objective, my goal, is to focus on the indictment and deal with the indictment. As far as I'm concerned, all the rest is a waste of time, and I believe that we're wasting a lot of time with these marginal issues. It would be better to spend our time with Ms. Tabeau. What she's telling us is extremely interesting. What you're saying during your cross-examination is also something we have to listen to, and we should not continue wasting our time on these marginal issues. But we'll check with the Registry and we'll try to see what's happening. Please proceed with your cross-examination. We still have ten minutes before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: These are just a few examples. There are a series of others, and there are also many examples of persons who declared themselves as Croats in 1991 and as Hungarians in 1992. There are some who declared themselves as Croats in 1991, and in 2002, they said that they are not declaring their ethnicity, that they haven't decided, that they're undecided. There are some who declared themselves in 1991 as Croats, and in 2002, they said that they simply did not wish to declare themselves, and then they were registered as unknown, unknown ethnicity. You know that there's a rubric like that, too. So if one were to work conscientiously on this material pertaining to censuses, one could clearly establish which Croats lived in 1991 in Hrtkovci and which ones left; isn't that right, Ms. Tabeau?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, seven names of Croats who changed their report, you are saying, in 2002, it's a very small number. An interesting issue would be to see whether there were any Serbs who changed their ethnicity into Croat in 2002. But I guess there are no such cases in the 2002 census, because this wouldn't make much sense in Vojvodina, dominated by the Serb population. In difficult times, nobody would like to be reported as a Croat, of course; that is, a non-Serb. But that is not the point I wanted to make. These are all a few examples of things that we agreed on this morning, and the major point is whether or not there were departures and when of Croats and other non-Serbs from Hrtkovci. I don't think the examples you gave us challenge the results of my report in any way. I don't see that there's a significant impact of these examples on the results presented in my report; not at all. I never said that all Croats left Hrtkovci. That is not true. Not all of them left, and it is possible that those who stayed reported themselves as Serbs in the 2002 census. Why not? The ethnicity of a Serb at that time was most certainly something that likely would give people a feeling of being more safe. So that's okay. There are a few people who report themselves in a different way in the 2002 census. That's all. So what?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But your task was to establish how many Croats had left Hrtkovci, when they left and why they left, and you did not fulfill that task because you didn't want to use relevant statistical sources; rather, you used auxiliary and highly unreliable sources. We had a witness here in the courtroom who went through Marko Kljajic's list and who established which people got certificates of baptism or birth certificates and hadn't left Hrtkovci at all. We had that kind of competent witness here, sitting where you're sitting now, and you must know who that witness is, so that I don't mention his name. Do you know who that is? Do you know we had a witness like that, very competent for that matter?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would prefer you told me because I'm not watching the court proceedings every day. If somebody has done this, has gone through the list, and based on I would like to know what, indicating who left, who stayed. I would be happy to know this, this person, the 280 names checked like this, and based on what? I would like to know if this person is aware of the fate of all 280 families? That would be, in my view, quite impressive. It's quite a lot of work to do, to make yourself familiar with the fate of 280 families.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Had you prepared for this testimony conscientiously, and since you're an OTP official, you had all of this made available to you. You could have followed the testimony of witnesses who testified about Hrtkovci, you had transcripts at your disposal, and now you want me to provide information to you. No. I'm not going to provide that kind of information to you because you haven't deserved that either through your professionalism or through your moral standing. Now we're going to move on to a different set of questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Your Honour. Mr. Seselj's comments about the witness's moral standing is completely inappropriate under these circumstances, and we strongly object to his characterizations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you've already been told over and over again not to have any biased qualifiers for witnesses that are under oath. You can say that you don't agree with the report for such-and-such reason. You can do that, but do not insult this person's morality or opinions or so forth. Ms. Biersay is absolutely right in taking the floor and making an objection.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I am concerned, Ms. Biersay is always right. But, all right, I'm not going to do that ever again. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Biersay is not finished.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, since I'm on my feet, I also wanted to make, for the record, the Prosecution's objection to not having been provided information, presumably by an expert that was retained by Mr. Seselj. Taking his argument that he was not able to get a copy of the report, it is unfair to the Prosecution to commence cross-examination without the information which clearly he's reading off a list. We would request that information be provided to the OTP. The second issue pertains to the private information given through the JMBG, and we would ask that those, perhaps because they are personal identifying numbers, that perhaps they should be redacted from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm absolutely opposed to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, we do not really know how things work in your own country, according to your law, but you probably know this. Regarding the census, we'd like to know whether this is public data or private data that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All this information is public, and when this information is requested, the requesting party has to have a justified reason. In principle, they're public. If a journalist is seeking them, the state authority is duty-bound to provide them. Then also if a person who has a particular interest is seeking them, then the state organ is duty-bound to provide this information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But there's supposed to be a justified reason, so it's not available for anyone. It's not --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may, census records are confidential. They are protected by confidentiality laws, especially names; and JMBG, which contains the date of birth of the person, recorded sex of the person, the region of birth of the person. This is all very personal information, and this information is not supposed to be shared in public sources. I know this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. To be on the safe side, we will redact this excerpt. I trust you on this, Ms. Tabeau. Mr. Seselj said something, and we also trust him, but since there is a contradiction, we will be extremely prudent and --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, there is no reason whatsoever to strike from the record this information if they do not tarnish the reputation or honour of an individual. Declaring oneself in ethnic terms was a free thing in Yugoslavia. Everyone could declare themselves whichever way they wanted to. Some people, by way of a joke, declared themselves to be Japanese, Indonesian, whatever; and no one can hold anyone responsible as to why they had declared themselves in a particular way once and then in a different way some other time. These constant interventions in the transcripts keep infringing upon the transparency of these proceedings. The OTP simply don't like my strong argumentation, and that's why they want to have it redacted. I ask you to keep it in the transcript as recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had already dealt with this this morning. I already mentioned this, your argument, and Ms. Tabeau confirmed this. She did say that some people could say that they were Croats in one census and declare themselves Serbs in the other census. We understand that and it's on the record, but we want to protect the people that you mentioned as examples. They might not want to be quoted. Maybe they don't want anyone to know that they changed their ethnicity. They probably don't want to see their JMBG number made public. There could be a problem with this, but to be on the safe side, we will redact. If later on we find out this wasn't necessary, we'll lift all this. What was important for the publicity of this hearing is that your argument be made and the answer also be put on the transcript, and that is on the transcript. But we will redact the names and the figures. It's now time for a break, it's 10 to 12.00, and we will resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have one hour left for this morning.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Shall I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau, you didn't answer my question. Why, for a full four years, did you not ask to be allowed to access the database of the Republican Institute for Statistics for Serbia?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did ask in 2004, in October, as I told you; and since then, I haven't repeated this request. This is all I can say. Why I didn't? It didn't cross my mind that the position on this could have changed, I guess, in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, how didn't it occur to you to do that, when the situation in Serbia and the authorities' reaction to The Hague Tribunal changed, and that almost all the accused had been extradited in one way or another, and that police archives have been opened, police files. Everything that The Hague asked for the Serb authorities provide them with immediately, and it never crossed your mind that that was possible? Ms. Tabeau, you have neglected this project. You didn't think it was serious enough, particularly serious, and you didn't know what was to be expected of you in court. Had you known what you would come up against in court, you would have prepared more thoroughly. Am I right in saying all that, had you been aware of all the challenges here?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I believe I have prepared very thoroughly and my report is a very thorough report. I want to draw the attention to the fact that the report is dated as of 2006. So it was long ago when the report needed to go finished and submitted, and this is what I did. I don't know about -- exactly about what has been made available recently by the Serb authorities to this Tribunal; but in my view, these are the latest developments that don't last for more than a couple of months, latest months, and not date back in 2006, when my deadlines were represented to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you did have the possibility subsequently of adding to your report and you could even enter corrections, and you could do that even the day before yesterday. You could do that; right? In your proofing session with the Prosecution, you could have entered some corrections had you been doing your work conscientiously; right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about corrections that you are suggesting to be made in the report. I believe my report is finished, a finished product, and I didn't make any corrections, except for annex A, in which dates of birth, a number of them, were corrected. Well, if this is the wish of this Chamber, I will be happy to update my report by requesting the census data once again and the relevant records on IDPs and refugees from the Serb authorities, and redo this report for Hrtkovci in the way as we discussed this morning. So such an update, once the data is provided, wouldn't take long, but I wouldn't expect a major shift in the patterns presented in my current report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, you don't assume, Ms. Tabeau, that I would have the patience to deal with you again here, if you were to write your report again. You had four years at your disposal, you didn't do it, you didn't avail yourself of any reliable sources. You turned towards unreliable sources, and now here you're glorifying the church books as reliable sources. It is a source for historical demography, that is true, and it is a source in states in which the church has the status of a legal cooperation. That was what the Kingdom of Yugoslavia was like, that it had public authorisation to keep the records. However, in communist Yugoslavia from 1945 onwards, the church was not a public and legal corporation and had no legal authority. Is that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't really matter what was the status, legal status, of the church, whether it had a legal corporation with the legal authority in the former Yugoslavia, because what did and does matter is that the church has been taking records of major vital events in their books. And I'm speaking of births and related christening records, and marriages, and related marriages, marriage records, and the notes for request for certificates. This is what was needed for this report, and this is what really matters. And from this point of view, the church books is a wonderful source of information, and a very, very long-term perspective one. So it not only provides with the latest data that are required for this study, but also makes it possible to place the data, recent data from the 1990s, in a long-term perspective. That is why I used this source. It's just a very good source from the point of view of the needs of this project.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That is absolutely untrue, everything you've said now. From 1945 onwards, the church did not keep records of births. It did of baptisms, and it kept the books of marriages exclusively for those who were married in church, and the law did not recognise church weddings, church marriages, but marriages concluded in front of state organs. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- it happens I was born and was growing in a socialist country, in Poland, and I know exactly how things were done under the socialism in Poland and what was the position of the Catholic Church in Poland. Well, first of all, church books have always registered the records of christenings and marriages; and as part of the record of christening, or baptism, as it is called as well, the date of birth of a child is available. And as part of the book of marriages, also exact information about the bride and the bridegroom is available, including birth date, name of parents, et cetera, et cetera. So from this point of view, the information is there in the books, and it lasts for a far longer period than the post-Second World War period. Church books is a rich source of information in historical perspective. Church books go back hundreds of years. In countries as Poland, which is a Catholic country in the first place, it is exactly --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Don't repeat that. There's no point in saying that. You've said it three or four times already. Do you imagine I don't know where church books are kept? You've told us that umpteen times. I'm talking about the situation in Serbia and Yugoslavia from 1945 onwards. In Poland, were church marriages from 1945 onwards recognised in Poland; were they? Give me a yes-or-no answer. Was it sufficient for you to get married in a church and then you've done with the marriage ceremony? Was that the case? You can just say "yes" or "no."

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: You had to have two marriages, in the municipality and in the church, in order for the marriage to be recognised. Church marriages alone wouldn't be recognised, indeed, but even --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: There we go.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't finish. If I may finish. Even the --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I'm really not interested in what you're going to say further. You've answered my question. That was what I was interested in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, please let the witness finish her answer. You've put a question to her. She's responding, but you're cutting her off; maybe because you don't like what she's saying. But let her finish her answer. What did you want to say, Madam?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm not interested in Poland and I don't want to expand about Poland. I was never interested in Poland, for that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you are an intelligent man. You know full well that she dealt with that by saying that in communist countries, and she's familiar with this system because she was born in Poland, things were organised in such-and-such way. Churches in Poland would record baptisms and marriages, including dates of births. So things were done that way in Poland. If it was done that way in Poland, it was probably done the same way in Czechoslovakia, in East Germany, and so on and so forth. That's the background of this explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What happened? Fire, not a real fire. It's a fire drill. Security measures are currently being checked as part of this drill. We are going to adjourn for now. If we're allowed to come back, we'll come back before a quarter past 1.00; otherwise, we'll continue tomorrow. It's a drill, it's a fire drill. Let's hope that we'll not burn alive, so we have to leave the courtroom.
